messages.subject: Is the bioconductor version the latest?
messages.subject_clean: Is the bioconductor version the latest?
messages.body_plain:
Hello
I have a possibly silly question...
Where do I get the latest version of MethylKit?

I see the github page has only version 0.99 from 2016.
Bioconductor for R 4.3 has version 1.24.
Is the bioconductor version the latest? Where can If find out what the latest version is?

I ask because I am having a bunch of problems that I think may have been resolved long ago...
like when I try to run the correlation function, I cannot change the method to anything other than Pearson or it gives an error, stating that Pearson should be used but the manual says that spearmans is an option.

Regards
Ryan

messages.subject: Re: Is the bioconductor version the latest?
messages.subject_clean: Is the bioconductor version the latest?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

The version on Bioconductor is the latest.
We did not set automated releases on github, that's why there we still have the version from 2016.

If you are having issues with the latest version, it would be great if you could post them on github together with a small reproducible example.

Best,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: MethyKit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

Yes, I am still maintaining methylKit together with Altuna Akalin.
Usually the best way to seek help would be via e-mail to methylkit_...@googlegroups.com or post a question using the web interface.
For bugs and errors please open issues on the github issue tracker.

As you realized the unite function is meant to merge at least two samples and does not work with fewer. However if the information that you need is the chr ID, start, end and the methylation percentage, this you might aswell extract and calculate directly from the methylRaw object ('myobj'). You can extract the underlying data of an object using the ˋgetDataˋ function, this should give you a data.frame with chromosome ID, start, end, strand, coverage, numCs (#cytosines) and numTs (#thymines). Then you can simply calculate methylation percentage as #cytosines/(#cytosines + #thymines ).

Best,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: MethyKit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

If you are asking whether the coverage could be directly used in the calculations, then yes, it is basically the sum of cytosines and thymines.

If you want to know whether you should filter for a minimum coverage to include a certain base, then yes, we usually require egh single base to have a coverage of at least 10 reads to be kept.

I hope this answers your questions.

Best,
Alex
